title: US Tariffs on Canada’s auto industry expose US jobs and GDP
gist: Oxford Economics finds a proposed 50% US tariff on Canadian autos, trucks, and parts (effective start of 2027) would leave overall US GDP and employment impact minimal at the national level but sharply concentrated in Midwest states, with Kentucky, Michigan, and Indiana most exposed and two-thirds of the at-risk jobs sitting outside auto manufacturing itself — a pattern the report likens to the diffuse downstream damage from the 2018 steel tariffs.

insights.claim: A proposed 50% US tariff on imports of autos, trucks, and car parts from Canada, if implemented at the start of 2027, would disproportionately expose Midwest states — Kentucky, Michigan, and Indiana — rather than being evenly distributed across the US economy.
insights.speaker: Keith Mason
insights.so_what: Investors and policymakers tracking this tariff should watch state-level labor and manufacturing data in KY/MI/IN rather than national aggregates, which will understate the localized shock.
insights.quote: US States in the Midwest – Kentucky, Michigan, and Indiana – will be exposed disproportionately to President Donald Trump’s proposed 50% tariff on imports of autos, trucks, and car parts from Canada, should it be implemented at the start of 2027

insights.claim: Kentucky's job exposure to the proposed Canadian auto tariff is 3.7 times the national average, followed by Michigan at 3.5 times and Indiana at 3.2 times, reflecting each state's relative dependence on Canadian auto-parts procurement.
insights.speaker: Keith Mason
insights.so_what: These three states carry a quantified, ranked exposure multiple that can be used to size regional GDP and employment downside scenarios if the tariff proceeds.
insights.quote: Kentucky faces the highest exposure—relative to the national average, Kentucky jobs are 3.7 times more exposed given their stronger links to Canadian auto procurement—followed by Michigan (3.5x) and Indiana (3.2x)

insights.claim: Despite the concentrated state-level exposure, Oxford Economics assesses the overall US economic impact of the proposed Canadian auto tariff as minimal at the national level.
insights.speaker: Keith Mason
insights.so_what: National-level GDP or jobs figures will mask the policy's real cost, so the trade matters much more for regional exposure than for macro aggregates — a pattern likely to recur with other targeted tariffs.
insights.quote: While the overall U.S. economic impact of this proposed tariff remains minimal at the national level, the state-level effects will be heavily concentrated.

themes.theme: Supply-chain spillover beyond the protected industry

insights.claim: Canadian auto manufacturers' purchases of parts and other goods from US businesses support an estimated 0.12% of all US jobs, giving a baseline size to the cross-border employment link a 50% tariff would put at risk.
insights.speaker: Keith Mason
insights.so_what: 0.12% of US employment is the ceiling for jobs directly tied to this specific cross-border procurement channel, useful as a denominator when modeling downside job-loss scenarios.
insights.quote: Canadian auto manufacturers’ purchases of parts and other goods from US businesses support an estimated 0.12% of US jobs.

insights.claim: An estimated two-thirds of the US jobs exposed to the proposed Canadian auto tariff sit in sectors other than automotive manufacturing itself, indicating the risk is concentrated in upstream and downstream supply-chain industries rather than automakers.
insights.speaker: Keith Mason
insights.so_what: Analysts should look beyond automakers and parts plants to logistics, distribution, and ancillary suppliers when assessing which US businesses actually bear the tariff's job risk.
insights.quote: We estimate two-thirds of exposed jobs will be in sectors other than automotive manufacturing.

themes.theme: Historical precedent from the 2018 steel tariffs

insights.claim: The 2018 US steel tariff (25%, later raised to 50% in Trump's second term) protected the steel industry itself and boosted its jobs, but slowed job growth in steel- and aluminum-reliant downstream industries initially, and those downstream jobs declined outright once the tariff rose to 50%.
insights.speaker: Keith Mason
insights.so_what: This is the closest historical analog for the proposed auto tariff: protecting one industry can still net-negative employment once downstream users of the protected input are counted, and escalating the tariff rate compounds the downstream damage rather than just adding more protection.
insights.quote: Although the steel industry itself was protected (and saw a jobs boost), industries reliant on steel and aluminum saw jobs growth slow initially, declining outright during Trump’s second term, when the administration raised the tariff to 50%
